summary:
The project turns scientific mission data into a training experience: An Simulator collects public NASA telemetry, uses an ML.NET FastTree Quad-Ensemble to estimate fuel yield, exploration duration, crew survival and system reliability, and presents scenarios for the ISS, Moon and Mars. The game turns these decisions into an educational card game for children aged 7–12.
Players first choose cards to build and protect their bio-ship/spacial base and outpost. Then, on every exploration turn, they play cards to manage resources and must make a mission decision before advancing to the next turn. Those choices change power, oxygen, radiation, shielding, suit wear and the ML.NET predictions; the mission ends in a safe return or a specific failure condition.
The solution connects real science, live data and decision-making in an accessible experience, encouraging STEM curiosity, systems thinking and awareness of the challenges of keeping people alive away from Earth. The intended impact is to make life support, space weather and ISRU understandable and fun.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Players build a bio-ship/spacial base and outpost by choosing cards, then face a required mission decision on every turn before advancing. The game has ML.NET predictions for fuel yield, exploration time, crew survival and system reliability.

What benefits does it offer?

It makes life support, power, radiation and space-weather trade-offs concrete and approachable. The game supports STEM learning, systems thinking and collaborative discussion through play.

What impact is intended?

The project aims to help young learners understand the real constraints of exploring beyond Earth. It encourages curiosity about science, engineering and the decisions required to keep a crew safe.

Which tools and technologies were used?

It was used C#, .NET 11, Blazor WebAssembly, .NET MAUI, MudBlazor, ML.NET FastTree, public NASA and partners REST APIs, GitHub Pages and licensed multimedia assets. The model was trained from 240,000 synthetic telemetry samples with 36 features.

What is the creative aspect?

The creative approach connects a scientific mission simulator to an educational decision card game. Scientific signals become readable cards, resources and consequences instead of remaining abstract data.

Which factors did the team consider?

I've considered the 7–12 age range, accessibility, understandable rules, mission realism, data provenance, browser-WASM limitations, and generated offline-ready artifacts.
